explainers.title: Hello and welcome to Reflection
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. You have already grown two thinking skills this year: Research, finding things out carefully, and Analysis, looking closely at what you found and asking why. Now you reach a skill that is a little different, because it is all about you. It is called Reflection.

Here are all six thinking skills again, so you can see where this unit fits:

The first three skills point outwards, at the world. Reflection points inwards, at yourself and at your team. It means stopping after you have done something, looking back honestly, and asking: what did I learn, how have my ideas changed, and what did I do well in my group?

People reflect all the time, not just at school. A farmer looks back at a harvest to see what to do differently next season. A nurse thinks about how to comfort the next worried patient. A shopkeeper works out why one week sold better than another. All of them are reflecting. People who look back and learn from their own experience get better, faster, at almost everything. That is the skill you will build here.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way.
Analysis — looking closely at what you found and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn, how you work in a team, and how you have changed.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You learn in the Ehel Academy way, where three kinds of help work together. Reflection needs its own version of this, because reflection is really about teamwork, and teamwork needs real people.

So this unit has a clear rhythm. You do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions, and sometimes with your family at home. Then you think it over with your AI tutor, in your own time, and turn what you noticed into a clear, honest reflection.

Think of it like a football match. Your teacher session is the real game, where you play alongside your team. Your time with your AI tutor is the quiet talk afterwards, when a good player looks back and works out how to play even better next time. In the old way of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'share with the group'. In our way, you do that thinking with your AI tutor, and you carry your best ideas back to your real team.
bullets: You, at your own pace. Reflection is naturally a quiet, personal skill. You write your own reflections in your own time, thinking honestly about your own work. Nobody can do that part for you.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Your tutor is your reflection partner. Before a team task it helps you plan what you will do. Afterwards it helps you talk through what went well and what was hard, and helps you draft your written reflection until it is clear, honest and complete.
Your teacher and your team, about twice a week. This is where the real teamwork happens. You work face to face with your group on a shared project, take a team role, and see how a real team feels.

explainers.title: Meet Idris and his team
explainers.body:
To make each part of reflection clear, we will follow one Year 5 learner all through the unit. His name is Idris, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Idris is not on his own. He works in a small team with three classmates: Hodan, Faisal and Deeqa. Across the year, this team takes on one shared Challenge, and Idris keeps a journal of what he learns as it grows. We will watch the team work on three parts of the very same project:

You will also see Idris's team disagree, forget a job, and get a few things wrong. That is completely normal. Every real team has a few muddles. What makes Idris's team a good team is not that they never have problems. It is that they keep working together kindly, and afterwards they look back honestly and learn. Your own team will be just the same, and that is nothing to worry about.
bullets: Planting the shade trees — the team notices how hot and bare the yard gets by midday, and plants a row of young trees along the fence.
The watering rota — the team makes a plan so the new trees are watered every day, even at weekends, while they are still too small to survive on their own.
Tree Day — the team teaches a younger class how to care for a tree, and shows the whole school what they have grown.

explainers.title: Your Challenge and your reflection journal
explainers.body:
In this unit you will not only read about Idris. You will do your own team Challenge, agreed with your group in a teacher session, and you will reflect on it just as he does. Your Challenge could be any shared project that matters where you live, such as growing shade trees, tidying a shared space, or helping younger children settle in.

To help you, start one simple habit that all good learners use: keep a reflection journal. This can be a notebook or a document where you write down what you learn about yourself and your team, a little at a time. It becomes the store of everything you notice, and it makes writing your final reflection far easier.

explainers.title: What is reflection, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think reflection just means saying 'that was good' or 'that was hard' and then moving on. Real reflection goes deeper than that. Reflection means thinking about an experience properly: what you learned, how your ideas changed, how your skills are growing, what you did for your team, and the good parts and the hard parts of working together.

Good reflection is always honest and balanced. Honest means you tell the truth about your own part, even the tricky bits. Balanced means you talk about what went well and what was hard, not just one or the other. A reflection that only praises you, or only complains, is not yet a strong reflection.

explainers.title: Reflecting on what you learned and how your ideas changed
explainers.body: One of the best things about a project is that it can change your mind. At the start you think one thing, and by the end, after you have tried it and found things out, you think something new. A strong reflection notices this change and says it clearly. A useful sentence frame is: I used to think ... but now I think ...

explainers.title: Reflecting on a skill you got better at
explainers.body: Every project helps you get better at something. It might be a big skill, like speaking to a group, or a smaller one, like keeping a fair rota or digging a straight, even hole. A strong reflection names one skill and says how you improved it and why you needed to. A useful frame is: Before I could not ... now I have got better at ... because I needed to ...

explainers.title: Your contribution to the team
explainers.body:
In a team, everyone should do something that helps. The thing you do is called your contribution. A strong reflection says clearly what you personally did, without either boasting or hiding.

Your contribution does not have to be the biggest or the loudest job. Quiet, steady help is just as valuable. Here are contributions that all really matter in a team:
bullets: Keeping clear notes so the team remembers its decisions.
Making sure a quieter member gets a turn to speak.
Watching the time so the team finishes what it planned.
Noticing a job that needs doing, and simply doing it.
Staying calm and kind when the team disagrees.

explainers.title: The benefits and challenges of teamwork
explainers.body: Working in a team has clear benefits, but it also brings real challenges. A balanced reflection is honest about both. If you only ever say teamwork is wonderful, or only ever say it is annoying, you are not reflecting fully.
bullets: Benefits: more ideas than one person could have alone, the work shared out so it is lighter, and different people who are good at different things.
Challenges: people disagree, someone may forget their part, it can take time to decide together, and it is hard to organise everyone at once.

explainers.title: Team roles: who does what
explainers.body:
Teams work better when everyone has a clear role. A role is a special job that helps the whole group. In Global Perspectives there are four roles that make teamwork run smoothly:

It is fair to swap roles between projects, so that everyone gets a turn at each. When you reflect, it helps to name your role, because your role shapes what you contributed and which skills you used.
bullets: Facilitator — makes sure everyone takes part and that the team stays friendly and on topic.
Recorder — keeps clear notes of what the team decides.
Reporter — tells the class or the assembly what the team found or made.
Timekeeper — watches the clock so the team finishes its work in the time it has.

explainers.title: Planning and fairly sharing the team's tasks
explainers.body:
A big project is really a set of smaller tasks. A good team lists the tasks, then shares them out fairly, so that no one person does everything and no one is left with nothing. A simple task plan answers four questions for each task: What needs doing? Who will do it? How will they do it? When, and how long will it take?

Clever teams also let some tasks happen at the same time, which we call working in parallel. While one person does one task, another does a different one, so the whole project finishes faster.

explainers.title: Writing a complete and balanced personal reflection
explainers.body:
Now you can put the parts together into a full personal reflection. A complete, balanced reflection covers all of these, in your own words:

That last point is the key to balance: a strong reflection always includes both the good and the hard. Leaving out the hard parts makes it sound boastful; leaving out the good parts makes it sound gloomy. Real reflection tells the whole story.
bullets: The project you worked on, and why it matters.
Your team's goal, and the action you took.
Your own contribution, told honestly.
How you could improve your contribution next time.
What was good about working as a team, and what was hard.

explainers.title: How new information and other people change your thinking
explainers.body: The deepest kind of reflection notices how you have changed because of a project. New facts and other people's ideas can change three things: what you think about the issue, how you behave, and the skills you have. A strong reflection can even explain the link between what you learned and what you then decided to do.
bullets: Your thoughts: Before, I used to think ... now I realise ... because ...
Your behaviour: Before I used to ... now I ... because I now know that ...
Your skills: Before I could not ... now I can ... because I needed to ...

explainers.title: Matching teamwork challenges to solutions
explainers.body: Every team meets challenges. The clever move is to notice the challenge and then find a sensible solution, so the same problem does not spoil your next project. Reflecting on a challenge is only really finished when you can say what you would do differently.

explainers.title: Giving constructive feedback
explainers.body: Sometimes you reflect on your own work, and sometimes you help someone else reflect on theirs by giving feedback. Good feedback is constructive, which means it is kind and helpful, and it always includes something that was done well and a clear idea for improving. Two friendly frames are: Well done for ... and Next time you could try ...

explainers.title: How Reflection makes your other skills stronger
explainers.body:
Reflection is special because it feeds back into every other skill. Each time you look back honestly, your next attempt at everything gets a little better.

So the honest thinking you do in this unit is never wasted. It is the skill that quietly lifts all the others.
bullets: Research improves when you reflect on which sources helped you and which wasted your time.
Analysis improves when you notice which of your reasons turned out to be strong.
Evaluation improves as you get better at judging your own work, not just other people's.
Collaboration improves the most, because reflecting on your teamwork shows you exactly how to be a better teammate.
Communication improves when you reflect on whether your audience really understood you.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: Idris's whole journey
explainers.body:
You have now met every part of reflection. Here is how they came together across Idris's team's Challenge, from a busy planting afternoon to a thoughtful, honest reflection.

He worked in a team on three parts of one Challenge: planting the shade trees, keeping the watering rota, and teaching a younger class on Tree Day. He took different roles, made a fair task plan, and noticed how his ideas about a 'finished' job changed. He wrote a complete, balanced reflection that named his contribution and both the good and the hard. By reflecting like this, Idris did not just finish a project. He became a stronger learner and a better teammate, ready for whatever comes next. In the Activities file, you will do the very same thing with your own team Challenge, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Collaboration. Reflection and Collaboration are close partners: reflection shows you how to work with others better, and collaboration gives you the real teamwork to reflect on. Everything you have practised here about roles, contributions, benefits and challenges will make you a much stronger member of any team. Well done for looking honestly at your own learning; that is one of the bravest and most useful things a learner can do.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: Reflection is like looking back at a garden you have grown, not just enjoying how it looks today. You look at what you did and what you learned, not just the result.
You cannot change what has already happened, but you can learn from it. Every honest reflection makes your next attempt a little better.
In this unit the tree project is the vehicle. The real prize is becoming someone who learns from everything they do.

bigIdeas.title: What to write in your reflection journal
lines: The date, and which part of the Challenge you worked on.
Your role in the team, and one thing you did to help.
One thing that went well, and one thing that was hard.
One way your ideas or your skills changed, however small.
One thing you want to do better next time.

bigIdeas.title: A model: what a complete reflection looks like
lines: The project we worked on was planting shade trees along the school fence, which matters because the yard gets very hot by midday.
Our goal was to plant five trees and keep them alive through their first year. The action we took was digging the holes, planting the saplings, and starting a watering rota.
My contribution was being the timekeeper at first, and then the reporter for Tree Day. I could have improved by checking the rota poster more often, so I would have noticed a missed day sooner.
Working as a team helped us because we could plant far more trees than one person could alone. It was challenging because we disagreed about where to plant the first tree, but we solved it by voting.
I used to think planting a tree was a job you finish in an afternoon, but now I know it is really the start of a much longer job of caring for it.

bigIdeas.title: A reflection to check
lines: Our team worked on planting shade trees at school. Our goal was to plant five trees. I dug the biggest hole and everyone said it was the best one. I think I did a great job.
Now check it against these questions. For each one, write 'yes' or 'no':

bigIdeas.title: Your team Challenge runs through everything
lines: With your group, agree one shared project that matters where you live, such as planting trees, tidying a shared space, or helping younger children settle in.
You will reflect on this same Challenge in every activity, so choose something you all care about.
By the end you will have a complete, honest reflection you can be proud of.

toolkit.title: The Reflection skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Reflection means thinking about an experience in depth: what you learned, how your ideas and behaviour changed, how your skills are growing, what you did for your team, and the good parts and the hard parts of working together. It is not just saying 'that was fun' and moving on.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always be honest about your own part, including the tricky bits. Second, always be balanced, talking about what was good and what was hard. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

Why bother? Because reflection is how you get better on purpose. Anyone can finish a project and move on. A learner who stops to think 'what worked, what did not, and what will I change next time' improves far faster. Every honest reflection makes your next team, your next project and your next attempt a little stronger.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 5 Reflection learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your reflection skills grow across three stages this year. Here are your real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these with you.

toolkit.title: The four team roles
toolkit.intro: Teams work best when everyone has a clear role. Swap roles between projects so everyone gets a turn at each.

rows: Facilitator
Makes sure everyone takes part and the team stays friendly and on topic.
Deeqa has not spoken yet; let's hear her idea.
Recorder
Keeps clear notes of what the team decides.
So we agreed to plant five trees along the fence. I have written that down.
Reporter
Tells the class or the assembly what the team found or made.
Our team found that the yard has no shade at all by midday.
Timekeeper
Watches the clock so the team finishes in the time it has.
We have five minutes left, so let's agree the spacing now.

toolkit.title: Template: planning and sharing the tasks
toolkit.intro:
Break your project into small tasks, then share them out fairly. Let some tasks happen at the same time (in parallel) to finish faster. Copy this grid and fill in one row per task.

Then check two things: is the share fair, and could any tasks be done in parallel to save time?

rows: Choose where to dig
Dig the holes
Water the saplings in
Put up stakes to protect them

toolkit.title: Frame: a complete and balanced personal reflection
toolkit.intro:
A strong reflection covers every part below. Finish each sentence starter in your own words, and always include both the good and the hard.

To show how you have changed, add one or two of these:
items: The project we worked on was ...
This project is important because ...
Our goal was ...
The action we took was ...
My contribution was ...
I could have improved my contribution by ...
Working as a team helped us to ...
Working as a team was challenging because ...
I used to think ... but now I think ...
Before I could not ... now I have got better at ... because ...
Before I used to ... now I ... because I now know that ...

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for benefits and challenges
toolkit.intro: Use these to talk in a balanced way about teamwork. Always give at least one of each.
items: A benefit was that working as a team let us ...
Another good thing about our teamwork was ...
A challenge we met was ...
This was hard because ...
Next time we could make it easier by ...

toolkit.title: Table: teamwork challenges and solutions
toolkit.intro: When you name a challenge in your reflection, follow it with a solution. This table gives common ones.

rows: We were not sure if the trees were actually growing well.
Decide how to measure it before you start, such as checking the height every two weeks.
We spent time worrying about a problem that was not really there.
Ask someone who knows, like the caretaker or a gardener, before deciding.
People had different ideas and some jobs were left undone.
Make a clear task plan saying who does what and by when.
We could not water the trees because it was a school holiday.
Make a rota that includes weekends and holidays, and ask families to help.
Others did not know what our team was doing.
Put up a small sign explaining the project.
People did not want to take a turn on the rota.
Show them how much the trees have already grown because of the rota.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for constructive feedback
toolkit.intro:
Good feedback is kind and helpful. Name a strength and an improvement. Use these starters:

Avoid feedback that is empty ('It was fine') or harsh ('That was bad'). Aim for the honest, kind middle.
items: Well done for ...
One thing you did really well was ...
Next time you could try ...
It might be even stronger if ...
Have you thought about ...?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for showing you have changed
toolkit.intro: Use these to show how a project changed your thoughts, your behaviour, or your skills:
items: Before, I used to think ... now I realise ... because ...
Before I used to ... however, now I ... because I now know that ...
Before I could not ... now I can ... because I needed to ...
Another person's idea changed my mind when ...

toolkit.title: Quick checklist: is my reflection strong?
toolkit.intro: Before you finish a reflection, read it back and tick each line. If you cannot tick them all, add the missing part.
items: It names the project and why it matters.
It gives the goal and the action the team took.
It describes my own contribution honestly, without boasting or hiding.
It says how I could improve my contribution next time.
It includes something that was good AND something that was hard.
It shows one clear way my ideas or my skills have changed.

checklists.title: Checklist: my part in the team (give yourself a score)
checklists.intro: Your contribution is your part — what you add to the team. Score yourself honestly for each way of helping, from 5 (I always did this) down to 1 (not yet). An honest low score shows you exactly what to work on.
items: I listened carefully to others
I made helpful suggestions
I kept my focus on the task
I helped my team to agree
I did my share of the work, even the less exciting jobs

challenge.intro: A balanced reflection is honest about the good parts and the hard parts of teamwork. This activity helps you capture both, so your final reflection tells the whole story.
topics: Think about your team Challenge so far. Write one clear benefit: something that was better because you worked as a team, not alone.
Now write one clear challenge: something that was harder because you worked as a team.
For your challenge, write one idea for making it smaller next time.
Finish this sentence honestly: 'On the whole, working as a team was worth it because ...'.
checkpoints: The most important thing I learned about myself is ...
The most important thing I learned about teamwork is ...
The one thing I will do differently in my next team is ...

activities.title: Start your reflection journal
activities.label: Activity 1: Start your reflection journal
activities.intro: A reflection journal is where you store what you learn about yourself and your team. Start yours now, and you will thank yourself later, because your final reflection will almost write itself.
steps: Write today's date and the name of your team Challenge at the top of a new page.
Write one sentence: 'The reason our team chose this Challenge is ...'.
Write one thing you are looking forward to about working in this team, and one thing you feel unsure about.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your team Challenge and your two feelings from step 3.
Ask it: What is one thing I could do to make the part I feel unsure about go better?
Ask the tutor to remind you what makes a reflection journal useful.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Share your Challenge with your group and agree it together in your next teacher session.
Agree how often you will each add to your own reflection journals.

activities.title: Assign your team roles
activities.label: Activity 2: Assign your team roles
activities.intro: Teams run smoothly when everyone has a clear role. Remember the four roles: facilitator (makes sure everyone takes part), recorder (keeps notes), reporter (tells the class), and timekeeper (watches the clock).
steps: Write the four roles in your journal, with one sentence saying what each one does.
Decide which role would suit you best right now, and which would stretch you the most.
Write one thing you would do to carry out your chosen role well.

boxes.title: A model: how one team shared the roles
lines: One Grade 5 team, working on a litter-clearing project, agreed roles at the start. Yasmin was the facilitator, so she made sure the quietest member always got a turn. Omar was the timekeeper, and gave a warning when five minutes were left.
The recorder kept notes of every decision, and the reporter told the class what the team had found. Because each person had one clear job, nobody was left out and nothing important was forgotten.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which role you would like and which would stretch you.
Ask it to help you plan how to do a stretching role well, so you feel ready to try it.
Ask the tutor why it is fair for a team to swap roles between projects.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Agree who will take each role for your Challenge, making sure the choice is fair.
Plan to swap roles next time so everyone gets a turn at each.

activities.title: Plan and fairly share the tasks
activities.label: Activity 3: Plan and fairly share the tasks
activities.intro:
A big project is a set of smaller tasks. Plan them with a simple grid that answers four questions: What needs doing, Who will do it, How they will do it, and When, and how long it will take. Try to let some tasks happen at the same time, which is called working in parallel.

Copy this grid into your journal and fill in one row for each task your Challenge needs.

When your grid is full, check it is fair: has anyone been given far too much, or too little? Change the grid until the share feels even.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your task grid to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Are any tasks shared unfairly, and which ones could we do in parallel to save time?
Ask the tutor to suggest a sensible order for the tasks.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Agree the real task grid together, and write down who has promised to do what.
Halfway through the project, check in with each other to see how the tasks are going.

activities.title: 'I used to think ... now I think ...'
activities.label: Activity 4: 'I used to think ... now I think ...'
activities.intro: One of the clearest signs of learning is a changed mind. This activity captures how your ideas have grown during your Challenge.
steps: Think back to the very start of your Challenge. Write one thing you believed about it then.
Now write what you believe about it today, after finding things out.
Join them with the frame: 'I used to think ... but now I think ...'.
Write one sentence saying what taught you the new idea (a fact, an experience, or another person).

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Idris wrote: I used to think planting a tree was a job you finish in one afternoon, but now I think it is really the start of a much longer job, because I learned that a young tree needs watering and care for a long time before it can look after itself.
What taught him the new idea: seeing one of the saplings wilt after a weekend nobody had watered it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your 'I used to think ... but now I think ...' sentence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your changed idea is clear, and what made it change.
Ask the tutor to help you notice one more way your thinking has grown this year.

activities.title: Which skill does the reflection show?
activities.label: Activity 5: Which skill does the reflection show?
activities.intro: A reflection can show any of the six Global Perspectives skills. Read each statement below and decide which skill it shows: Research, Analysis, Evaluation, Reflection, Collaboration, or Communication. Write the pairs, such as 1-Analysis.
steps: 'I checked whether the online article that said young trees do not need much water could be trusted, and found it had no author.'
'I worked out that the real reason the trees were struggling was not enough water, not too much sun.'
'The question our team investigated was: how much water does a young tree actually need each week?'
'I made sure everyone in the group had a turn to hold the watering can.'
'I looked back and noticed my idea about tree planting had completely changed.'
'I explained our watering rota to the whole school at assembly, clearly and simply.'

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain, simply, any that you found tricky.
Then ask the tutor: which of these six skills do I most want to get better at, and why?

activities.title: The watering rota, and a teamwork problem
activities.label: Activity 6: The watering rota, and a teamwork problem
activities.intro: A young tree needs watering every day until it is established, so Idris's team had to build a rota — a plan that shares a job fairly, taking turns. Match each problem (1 to 4) to the best solution (A to D). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
steps: Everyone wants the easy watering day, and nobody wants the weekend.
The team forgot to write down whose turn it was to water.
One teammate missed their day and nobody noticed until a tree wilted.
A new teammate joined the project and did not know the rota.
A. Write the rota on a poster everyone can see, with each name against each day.
B. Share out the days fairly, including weekends, and ask families to help when needed.
C. Agree that if someone cannot do their day, they must tell someone else in good time.
D. Show the new teammate the rota and explain it clearly before their first turn.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four pairs to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it which problem your own team is most likely to meet, and why.
Ask the tutor to help you plan ahead so that problem is smaller next time.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Agree the real watering rota together, including who covers weekends.
If someone cannot do their day, agree how they will tell the rest of the team in good time.

activities.title: Sort the reflections: benefit, or challenge?
activities.label: Activity 7: Sort the reflections: benefit, or challenge?
activities.intro: A balanced reflection names both a benefit and a challenge of teamwork. Read what Idris's team said after planting the trees, and sort each sentence.
steps: A. We could never have planted five trees in one afternoon on our own.
B. We disagreed about where the trees should go, and it took a while to decide.
C. Different people noticed different problems, so between us we thought of more solutions.
D. It was hard to get everyone to remember their watering day.
Write which group each sentence belongs to: benefit or challenge.
Now write one real benefit and one real challenge from your own team's Challenge.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your benefit and your challenge to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your reflection is balanced, with both a good part and a hard part.
Ask the tutor for one more benefit of teamwork that you may not have noticed.

activities.title: Tree Day: giving constructive feedback
activities.label: Activity 8: Tree Day: giving constructive feedback
activities.intro: For Tree Day, Idris's team teaches a younger class how to care for a tree, and shows the whole school what they have grown. Afterwards, teammates give each other constructive feedback: kind, specific, and helpful.
steps: Read the weak reflection in the box below.
Write one thing the teammate did well, using the frame 'Well done for ...'.
Write one clear idea for improving it, using the frame 'Next time you could try ...'.
Check your feedback is kind, specific and helpful, not empty and not harsh.

boxes.title: A weak reflection to respond to
lines: A teammate wrote: 'I helped water the trees. It was good. I do not really know what else to say.'

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your feedback to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your feedback is kind, specific and helpful.
Ask the tutor to show you one other polite way to suggest an improvement.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Plan Tree Day together: who teaches the younger class, and who speaks at the assembly.
Practise your parts together before the real day.

activities.title: Write your complete personal reflection
activities.label: Activity 9: Write your complete personal reflection
activities.intro: Now put every part together. Use the frame from your Skills Toolkit to write a full, honest, balanced reflection on your own team Challenge, covering the project, your goal, your contribution, and both the good and the hard.
steps: Write one or two sentences for each part of the frame: the project, why it matters, your goal, your contribution, and how you could improve it.
Write one benefit and one challenge of working as a team.
Write one clear way your ideas or your skills have changed.
Read your reflection back against the Quick checklist in your Skills Toolkit, and add anything missing.
Finish your three checkpoint sentences below.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full reflection to your AI tutor.
Ask it: is my reflection complete, honest and balanced? Which part is strongest, and which is weakest?
Ask the tutor to help you improve the weakest part until you are proud of the whole reflection.

practice.partTitle: Fix these weak reflections
practice.intro: Read each weak reflection below and rewrite it so it is stronger: give a goal, a contribution, and both something good and something hard.
practice.prompt: A teammate wrote: 'Planting the trees was good. I liked it.' Rewrite this as a stronger reflection.
practice.answer: Our goal was to plant five shade trees along the fence. I helped by digging one of the holes and carrying water. It went well because everyone worked together and we finished in one afternoon. It was hard because the ground was very dry and hard to dig, so next time we would soften it with water first.

practice.partTitle: Fix these weak reflections
practice.prompt: A teammate wrote: 'The watering rota was annoying. Nobody did their job properly.' Rewrite this as a stronger, more balanced reflection.
practice.answer: Our watering rota helped us share the job of caring for the trees fairly. It was challenging because two people missed their day at the weekend, so a couple of the trees wilted a little. We fixed it by putting the rota on a poster by the gate, and asking families to remind us.

practice.partTitle: Fix these weak reflections
practice.prompt: A teammate wrote: 'I was the reporter. I told the school about the trees. That's it.' Rewrite this as a stronger reflection about their role.
practice.answer: As reporter, I told the whole school assembly about our tree project on Tree Day. My contribution was practising my talk with my team beforehand, so I could speak clearly and not too quickly. It went well because the younger children asked lots of questions afterwards, which showed they had listened.

practice.partTitle: Is this reflection honest and balanced?
practice.intro: Read each reflection below and decide whether it is honest and balanced.
practice.prompt: Read: 'Our team was amazing. We never disagreed about anything and everyone did their job perfectly.' Is this a balanced reflection? Explain your answer.
practice.answer: No. It only says good things and does not mention anything hard or anything that could be improved, so it is not balanced. A real team almost always disagrees about something.

practice.partTitle: Is this reflection honest and balanced?
practice.prompt: Read: 'Everything about our tree project went wrong. It was a waste of time.' Is this a balanced reflection? Explain your answer.
practice.answer: No. It only says bad things and does not mention anything that went well, so it is not balanced either. Even a difficult project usually has something that worked.

practice.partTitle: Is this reflection honest and balanced?
practice.prompt: Read: 'I dug a hole. Faisal watered it. The end.' Is this reflection complete? What is missing?
practice.answer: No, it is not complete. It only lists actions and is missing the goal, what was learned, and how anyone's ideas or skills changed.

practice.partTitle: Is this reflection honest and balanced?
practice.prompt: Read: 'Our goal was five trees. I was the timekeeper and made sure we finished before the bell. It went well because we planted all five, but it was hard because we argued about where to dig first.' Is this reflection balanced and complete? Explain your answer.
practice.answer: Yes. It names the goal, the contribution, something good, and something hard, so it is both balanced and complete.

practice.partTitle: Spot the parts of a reflection
practice.intro: Read each sentence and name which part of a reflection it shows.
practice.prompt: In the sentence 'My contribution was keeping the watering rota poster up to date,' which part of a reflection is this?
practice.answer: This is the learner's personal contribution — what they themselves did to help the team.

practice.partTitle: Spot the parts of a reflection
practice.prompt: In the sentence 'Working as a team helped us because we could plant far more trees than one person alone,' which part of a reflection is this?
practice.answer: This is a benefit of teamwork.

practice.partTitle: Spot the parts of a reflection
practice.prompt: In the sentence 'It was hard because we disagreed about where to plant the first tree,' which part of a reflection is this?
practice.answer: This is a challenge of teamwork.

practice.partTitle: Spot the parts of a reflection
practice.prompt: In the sentence 'I used to think a tree was fully grown once it was planted, but now I know it needs years of care,' which part of a reflection is this?
practice.answer: This shows how the learner's ideas changed because of new information or experience.

practice.partTitle: Match the teamwork problem to a solution
practice.intro: Match each teamwork problem to a sensible solution.
practice.prompt: Problem: 'Everyone wants the easy watering day, and nobody wants the weekend.' What is a sensible solution?
practice.answer: Share out the days fairly, including weekends, and ask families to help when needed.

practice.partTitle: Match the teamwork problem to a solution
practice.prompt: Problem: 'The team forgot to write down whose turn it was to water.' What is a sensible solution?
practice.answer: Write the rota on a poster everyone can see, with each name against each day.

practice.partTitle: Match the teamwork problem to a solution
practice.prompt: Problem: 'One teammate missed their day and nobody noticed until a tree wilted.' What is a sensible solution?
practice.answer: Agree that if someone cannot do their day, they tell someone else in good time.

practice.partTitle: Match the teamwork problem to a solution
practice.prompt: Problem: 'A new teammate joined the project and did not know the rota.' What is a sensible solution?
practice.answer: Show the new teammate the rota and explain it clearly before their first turn.

practice.partTitle: How did the idea change?
practice.intro: Complete each reflection to show how an idea or a feeling changed.
practice.prompt: Idris used to think a tree just needed to be planted once and would then look after itself. What might have changed his mind, and what might he think now?
practice.answer: Seeing a young tree wilt because it was not watered for a few days probably changed his mind. He now thinks a young tree needs regular care and watering for a long time before it can survive on its own.

practice.partTitle: How did the idea change?
practice.prompt: Complete this reflection: 'I used to think working alone was faster than working in a team, but now I think...'
practice.answer: ...I think a team is often faster for a big job, because the work is shared out and different people can do different tasks at the same time.

practice.partTitle: How did the idea change?
practice.prompt: Complete this reflection: 'Before, I found it hard to speak in front of a group, but now...'
practice.answer: ...now I have got better at it, because my team let me practise my Tree Day talk with them first, so by the real day I felt much more confident.

practice.partTitle: Your own reflection
practice.intro: Now write your own answers. There is no single right answer for these — write honestly about your own team Challenge.
practice.prompt: Write one thing you did to help your own team Challenge, however small.
practice.note: Open reflection — compare your answer with your AI tutor instead of a fixed model answer.

practice.partTitle: Your own reflection
practice.prompt: Write one benefit and one challenge of working with your own team.
practice.note: Open reflection — compare your answer with your AI tutor instead of a fixed model answer.

practice.partTitle: Your own reflection
practice.prompt: Write one skill you have got better at this year, and how you improved it.
practice.note: Open reflection — compare your answer with your AI tutor instead of a fixed model answer.

practice.partTitle: Your own reflection
practice.prompt: Write one thing you would do differently if you did your Challenge again.
practice.note: Open reflection — compare your answer with your AI tutor instead of a fixed model answer.

reflection.prompt: Look back at your Challenge from the start. Write one thing you believed about it then, and one thing you believe now.
Name the role you took in your team, and write one thing you did in that role to help.
Write one benefit of working in a team, and one challenge, from your own Challenge.

Idris's team disagreed about where the first tree should go. Hodan said, 'It should go by the gate, so everyone sees it first.' Faisal said, 'It should go by the classroom, so it gives us shade at break.' Write one fair way the team could decide.
reflection.modelAnswer: A fair way would be to vote, or to ask which spot needs shade most and choose that one, so the decision is not just one person's choice.

reflection.prompt: Idris wrote: 'I used to think planting a tree was a job you finish in one afternoon. But now I think...' Finish his sentence in a way that fits what you have learned about the watering rota.
reflection.modelAnswer: ...I think planting a tree is really the start of a much longer job, because a young tree needs watering and care for a long time before it can look after itself.

reflection.prompt: Name one skill you have got better at this year, in Global Perspectives or anywhere else, and say how you improved it.
A teammate wrote: 'I did my part. It was fine.' Write one piece of kind, useful feedback for them.
reflection.modelAnswer: Well done for finishing your part — that really helped the team stay on time. Next time you could try adding one thing that was hard, so your reflection tells the whole story.

reflection.prompt: Write one thing your team could do differently next time you take on a shared project.
Explain, in your own words, why a good reflection needs to include both something good and something hard.
reflection.modelAnswer: Because only writing the good parts sounds boastful, and only writing the hard parts sounds gloomy. A true reflection is honest about the whole experience, not just the part that makes you look best.

reflection.prompt: What is the one thing you are proudest of from your team Challenge this year, and why?

vocabulary.meaning: Thinking carefully about something you have done, including what you learned and how you changed.
The part you personally did to help your team.
A good result that comes from something, such as working as a team.
Something that makes a task harder to do.
Including both the good parts and the hard parts, not just one.
Telling the truth about something, even the tricky parts.
People working together towards one shared goal.
A special job within a team that helps the whole group.
The team member who makes sure everyone gets a turn to speak.
The team member who keeps clear notes of what the team decides.
The team member who tells other people what the team found or made.
The team member who watches the clock so the team finishes in time.
One small job that is part of a bigger project.
Doing two or more tasks at the same time, so a project finishes faster.
A notebook where you write down what you learn about yourself and your team.
Kind, helpful comments that name something done well and something to improve.
The way one particular person sees or thinks about something.
The start of a sentence that helps you finish your own idea clearly.
A plan that shares a job fairly between people, taking turns.
A moment when you stop and check how something is going.

mistakes: Writing only the good parts of a reflection, and leaving out anything that was hard.
Writing only the hard parts, and forgetting to say what went well.
Saying 'it was fun' or 'it was hard' without saying why.
Forgetting to name your own contribution, and only describing what the whole team did.
Copying a teammate's reflection instead of writing your own honest one.
Giving feedback that only says 'good job' with nothing helpful to improve.
Naming a challenge but not saying what you would do differently next time.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I did to help my team.
I can explain one benefit and one challenge of working as a team.
I can say how new information changed what I thought.
I can say how another person's idea changed my thinking.
I can name a skill I have got better at, and say how.
I can write a reflection that includes both something good and something hard.
I can give kind, helpful feedback to a teammate.
I can match a teamwork problem to a sensible solution.
I can explain what my role in the team was, and what I did in it.
I can say one thing I would do differently next time.
